Control — Who is telling the truth? Pole placement versus small-signal models

Power Electronic Systems · HTWG · 2026 · Draft for teaching review
Prerequisites: Lesson 1 §7 and Exercise E4, the boost exercises of Lesson 2, and the control part of the circuit-foundations recap.

Two engineers get the same task: design the voltage controller of a DC/DC converter. The control engineer draws the LC filter, writes its state equations and places the closed-loop poles. The power-electronics engineer starts from the two switch positions, averages them over a switching period, finds the operating point and linearizes. They get two different transfer functions for the same circuit. Both say that their model is the plant.

Who is telling the truth? This lesson does not pick a winner. It shows when the two models are the same model, when they differ, and which omitted physics makes them differ. All numbers come from the Example script scripts/model_comparison.py, and its checks are in model-checks.json.

How this lesson is built. This lesson does not follow the design-led structure of Lessons 1 and 2. It compares models, and no single reference design shows every effect. It follows one live session of 90 minutes, in seven parts. The circuit values are teaching assumptions, not checked component selections. Each one is stated where it is used.

Learning outcomes and teaching route

By the end, students should be able to:

  • separate four activities that both engineers do: physical modeling, linearization, controller synthesis and implementation
  • derive the state-space model of an LC plant and place its poles by state feedback
  • derive the averaged and linearized model of a buck, a boost and a buck-boost from their two switch positions
  • say for each topology whether the duty cycle moves the poles, the zeros or only the gain
  • explain the right-half-plane zero of the boost and buck-boost physically, and say what it costs the controller
  • explain why a stiff-link inverter can often use the simple LC model, and when it cannot
  • check a linear model against a switching model and name the source of each error: the operating point, the size of the perturbation, averaging or delay.
Part Time Section Classroom question
1 00–10 §1 Two engineers, one converter If two models have the same poles, are they the same plant?
2 10–25 §2 The control engineer's model Does a controller need to know what drives the LC filter?
3 25–40 §3 The power-electronics model Where does the nonlinearity come from, if L and C are linear?
4 40–55 §4 Buck, boost and buck-boost Does the duty cycle move the poles?
5 55–70 §5 Inverters and motor drives Why does the simple model so often work for inverters?
6 70–85 §6 Which model predicts the switching converter? Which error is from the operating point, which from averaging?
7 85–90 §7 Quick check and conclusion Who was telling the truth?

§8 lists what to retain. §9 holds the training: one worked exercise and two assigned Exercises.

1. Two engineers, one converter

The control engineer. "The converter is an LC filter with a load. I write , check controllability and place the poles. The switching is fast. I can ignore it."

The power-electronics engineer. "The converter changes its topology twice per period. I average the two states, find the operating point and linearize. My transfer function changes with the duty cycle. A model with fixed LC poles is wrong."

Predict before reading on. Answer each question in one sentence. Keep your answers. §7 returns to them.

  1. If two models have the same poles, are their transfer functions the same?
  2. Can a controller move the poles of a converter without changing L or C?
  3. Does a converter that switches at 20 kHz have a pole at 20 kHz?

The disagreement is smaller than it sounds. Pole placement and small-signal modeling are not competing theories. Pole placement is a method to design a controller. Small-signal modeling is a method to get a linear plant. Each engineer does four separate things, and the disagreement is in the first two:

  1. Physical modeling. Which states, switch positions and energy stores does the model contain?
  2. Linearization. About which operating point is the model valid?
  3. Controller synthesis. How are the closed-loop poles, the bandwidth and the damping chosen?
  4. Implementation. What changes when the controller drives a real switched converter through a modulator with sampling and delay?
Question Passive-network model Averaged converter model
What is modeled? LC network and load Switch network, LC and load
Duty cycle An input gain, often hidden Part of the averaged dynamics
Operating point Not needed for a linear passive plant Needed for the linearization
Switching frequency Not represented Also not represented in the basic averaged model
Topology Often reduced to "a filter" Explicit: the switch network connects L and C
Controller design Pole placement, LQR, PID Pole placement, PI, PID, loop shaping
Main limit Can omit the converter's own dynamics Valid locally, and only as far as averaging holds

Note the third row. Neither model represents the switching frequency. The basic averaged model is just as blind to PWM delay, sampling and ripple as the LC model. Both need extra modeling for those effects (§6.4).

2. The control engineer's model: an LC plant and pole placement

2.1 The LC plant

Drive an LC filter with load R from a controllable voltage u. The states are the inductor current and the capacitor voltage, :

(2.1)

The state matrix A has the rows and . The input vector is .

The open-loop poles solve :

(2.2)

These are the natural frequencies of the passive plant. Nothing here knows how u is made.

2.2 State feedback places the poles

Feed back both states, . The closed loop is , and its characteristic polynomial is

(2.3)

Match it to . Two gains set two coefficients, so any pair of poles is possible. The plant must be controllable, and the duty cycle must not saturate. Lesson 1, Exercise E4 places the poles of a buck this way.

Pole placement changes the closed-loop dynamics. It does not repair a wrong plant model. The gains are only as good as A and B.

2.3 What if the input is a duty cycle?

A real controller does not command a volt. It commands a duty cycle. For an ideal buck the switch-node voltage averages to , so the input vector in duty units is .

The open-loop poles do not change. The duty-unit gains do depend on . Take the Lesson 1 teaching buck: 48 V, 60 µH, 100 µF, 2.4 Ω, and design for 2 kHz and = 0.7 at 48 V. Keep the gains fixed and let the input move:

Closed-loop Step overshoot DC gain
30 V 2021 Hz 0.50 16.7 % 0.61
48 V (design) 2000 Hz 0.70 4.6 % 1.00
60 V 1986 Hz 0.84 0.8 % 1.27

The poles barely move, but the damping and the reference gain do. A feedforward of in the modulator removes this effect. Voltage-mode controllers often provide it as a PWM ramp that scales with the input voltage.

The control engineer is not wrong. The model needs one more line: how the converter turns the controller output into the voltage u.

3. The power-electronics model: averaging and linearization

3.1 Two switch positions, one average

A switched converter has one set of linear equations for each switch position:

(3.1)

Average over one switching period. The switch is on for the fraction d:

(3.2)

When , the duty cycle multiplies a state. The averaged model is then nonlinear, although L and C are linear. The nonlinearity comes from the way the switch network connects them. This is the state-space averaging of Middlebrook and Ćuk (1976). Erickson and Maksimović develop it in chapter 7.

3.2 Linearize about the operating point

Write each quantity as its operating-point value plus a small deviation: , , . The operating point solves . Keep the first-order terms only:

(3.3)
  • holds the dynamics of the averaged plant at this duty cycle.
  • is the sensitivity to the input voltage.
  • is the sensitivity to the duty cycle. It contains the operating point X. The same circuit responds differently to at different loads and voltages.

The duty-to-output transfer function follows directly. With the output :

(3.4)

3.3 What the model assumes

Name the approximations before using the model:

  1. Averaging. The dynamics of interest are slow compared with the switching frequency. The ripple is small.
  2. Linearization. Products of two deviations are neglected. The perturbation must be small.
  3. One operating point, one conduction mode. The model holds for one D, one load and CCM.
  4. No switching detail. The model has no ripple, no sampling and no modulator delay.

A large change of operating point does not invalidate the nonlinear averaged model (3.2). It invalidates the idea that one linearization (3.3) is good everywhere. §6 measures each error separately.

4. Buck, boost and buck-boost: does the duty cycle move the poles?

Apply §3 to the three basic topologies. Write the averaged equations, then look at one thing: does d multiply a state?

Topology L C R Source
Buck 48 V 60 µH 100 µF 2.4 Ω 100 kHz Lesson 1, Appendix E and E4
Boost 100 V 1 mH 100 µF 100 Ω 20 kHz teaching values
Buck-boost 100 V 1 mH 100 µF 100 Ω 50 kHz teaching values

Each converter is checked in CCM at D = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. At 20 kHz the buck-boost leaves CCM at D = 0.2: its inductor current is 0.31 A, and half the ripple is 0.50 A. It therefore switches at 50 kHz. The boost at D = 0.8 delivers 500 V and 2.5 kW into the fixed 100 Ω. This is a fixed-load comparison, not a fixed-power one.

4.1 The buck: duty only scales the input

(4.1)

The duty cycle multiplies , which is not a state. With a constant input the averaged buck is already linear, and

(4.2)

At all three duty cycles the poles sit at = 2055 Hz with Q = 3.10, and the gain is 48 V. For the ideal buck, the control engineer's LC model and the averaged model are the same model. The passive LC model is not always wrong.

4.2 The boost: the duty cycle reflects the inductor

(4.3)

Now d multiplies both states: the products and . These two products are the origin of every difference that follows. Write . The operating point is

(4.4)

Linearize:

(4.5)

Eliminate :

(4.6)

Read the denominator. It is the LC polynomial with L replaced by . The switch network reflects the inductor to the output, weighted by the duty cycle. The control engineer's LC model is right in form, but it uses the wrong inductance. The poles and the zero are at

(4.7)

The numerator holds a zero in the right half-plane. Section 4.4 explains it.

4.3 The buck-boost: same poles, a different zero

Take as the magnitude of the inverted output. Then

(4.8)

The operating point is and . The same steps give

(4.9)

The low-frequency gain is the slope of the conversion ratio. Check it by differentiating. With the same L, C and R, the buck-boost has exactly the poles of the boost. Only its zero is higher, by the factor 1/D.

4.4 The numbers, and what they show

Topology D Gain Q RHP zero
Buck 0.2 9.6 V 4.0 A 48 V 2055 Hz 3.10 none
Buck 0.5 24 V 10 A 48 V 2055 Hz 3.10 none
Buck 0.8 38.4 V 16 A 48 V 2055 Hz 3.10 none
Boost 0.2 125 V 1.56 A 156 V 403 Hz 25.3 10.2 kHz
Boost 0.5 200 V 4.0 A 400 V 252 Hz 15.8 3.98 kHz
Boost 0.8 500 V 25 A 2500 V 101 Hz 6.3 637 Hz
Buck-boost 0.2 25 V 0.31 A 156 V 403 Hz 25.3 50.9 kHz
Buck-boost 0.5 100 V 2.0 A 400 V 252 Hz 15.8 7.96 kHz
Buck-boost 0.8 400 V 20 A 2500 V 101 Hz 6.3 796 Hz

The Example script checks each closed form above against a numerical Jacobian of the averaged model. Poles, zeros and gains agree to 10⁻⁶.

Three things change with D in the boost and the buck-boost, and none of them in the buck:

  1. The resonance moves. From D = 0.2 to 0.8 it falls by a factor of four, from 403 Hz to 101 Hz.
  2. The gain changes. It rises sixteen-fold, from 156 V to 2500 V. A fixed controller sees its loop gain change by 24 dB.
  3. The RHP zero moves down. It falls with , from 10.2 kHz to 637 Hz in the boost.

Two zeros in the table are out of the model's reach. The boost zero at D = 0.2 lies at 10.2 kHz, about half the 20 kHz switching frequency. The buck-boost zero at D = 0.2 lies at 50.9 kHz, above its switching frequency. Averaging assumes dynamics well below , so the model cannot predict a zero there (§3.3, point 1). §6 shows that the switching converter has no visible dip at D = 0.2.

4.5 Why the output first goes the wrong way

Predict. Increase the duty cycle of a boost in one step. Does the output voltage rise immediately?

It does not. A higher duty cycle keeps the switch on for longer. The inductor stores more energy, but the diode conducts for a shorter part of each period. In the first periods, the inductor current has not risen yet, and less charge reaches the output capacitor. The output falls. Only when the inductor current has grown does the output rise to its new value.

This inverse response is the time-domain picture of the RHP zero. The zero adds phase lag, as a pole does, while it raises the gain, as a zero does. No stable controller can remove it. A controller that cancelled it would need an unstable pole. In practice, the RHP zero limits the loop crossover. A common rule of thumb keeps the crossover below about one fifth of the lowest RHP-zero frequency in the operating range. Lesson 2 meets the same mechanism in the charging boost.

4.6 Design at one operating point, run at another

Now let the control engineer use the correct averaged model, but only at D = 0.5. Place the boost poles at 500 Hz with = 0.7, using state feedback in duty units, with a reference gain for unity DC gain. Keep the gains fixed and move the operating point:

Boost operating point Closed-loop poles Step overshoot Step undershoot DC gain
D = 0.2 583 Hz, = 0.39 26.6 % 0.2 % 0.73
D = 0.5 (design) 500 Hz, = 0.70 4.6 % 0.7 % 1.00
D = 0.8 real: 164 Hz and 1408 Hz 0 % 11.2 % 1.08

The loop stays stable, but it is a different loop at each end. At D = 0.2 it rings and misses its reference by 27 %. At D = 0.8 its slow pole sits at 164 Hz, and the RHP zero at 637 Hz is close enough to cause an 11 % undershoot. The duty cycle has moved the plant, and fixed gains cannot follow it. The usual remedies are gain scheduling with D, an inner current loop, and a crossover chosen for the worst operating point. Exercise E1 compares them for the buck-boost.

5. Inverters and motor drives: why the simple model often works

5.1 The inverter with a stiff DC link

A full-bridge inverter drives an LC output filter. Its averaged bridge voltage is , with the modulation index :

(5.1)

This is the buck equation (4.1) again, with in place of d. If is stiff, the modulation changes only the excitation. It does not change the filter poles. With 1 mH, 20 µF and 50 Ω the filter resonates at 1125 Hz with = 0.071, at every modulation index.

This is why inverter and motor-drive engineers can use LC models and state feedback with good results. Their converter is, to first order, a buck with a stiff source. The duty-dependent reflection of §4.2 never appears.

5.2 When the DC link is not stiff

Feed the DC link from a 400 V source through a source resistance = 2 Ω into a link capacitor = 50 µF. The link voltage is now a state:

(5.2)

Linearize the bridge voltage:

(5.3)

The operating point M now enters the dynamics, in (5.2) and in (5.3). This is the same mechanism as the boost: the modulation multiplies a state. The three-state model at a DC operating point gives:

M Filter resonance Filter DC-link pole
stiff link 400 V 1125 Hz 0.071 none
0.2 399.4 V 1129 Hz 0.074 1583 Hz
0.5 396.0 V 1150 Hz 0.092 1540 Hz
0.8 390.0 V 1191 Hz 0.123 1458 Hz

Here the effect is moderate: the resonance moves by 6 %, and its damping rises. But the DC link, the upstream rectifier and their own controllers now interact with the inverter. An LC-only model cannot show this interaction, because it contains neither the states nor the coupling. Exercise E2 asks how stiff the link must be.

5.3 The motor-drive model

A permanent-magnet synchronous machine in the rotor frame has

(5.4)

with the stator resistance , the electrical speed and the magnet flux linkage . The model assumes sinusoidal quantities, known parameters and the dq transformation. The speed-dependent cross-coupling terms are usually compensated by feedforward. Each current axis is then a first-order RL plant, driven by an inverter that the model treats as an ideal voltage source.

Motor-control engineering does not use an incomplete model. It uses the model that fits the dynamics it controls. The complete drive also has DC-link dynamics, dead time, modulator saturation, sampling delay and parameter changes with speed and current.

Ask. At which current-loop bandwidth does the "ideal controllable voltage source" stop being good enough? No single number answers this. The answer depends on the switching frequency, the PWM update method, the sampling and the robustness the drive needs. §6.4 gives the first estimate.

6. Which model predicts the switching converter?

A model is a claim about a physical system. Test the claim against something closer to the system than the model itself.

6.1 The experiment

Take the boost of §4. Compare three models with a fourth reference:

  • Model A: passive LC. Fixed 1 mH, 100 µF and 100 Ω, poles at 503 Hz with Q = 31.6. Its gain is matched at D = 0.5. It has no RHP zero.
  • Model B: averaged, linearized at D = 0.5. One model for all operating points.
  • Model B′: averaged, linearized at the actual D. One model per operating point.
  • Reference: the exact switching converter. The Example script solves the two linear switch-position equations exactly, period by period, from the periodic steady state. It plots the average over each switching period, so ripple does not hide the comparison.

All four use the same input and output: duty step = 0.005, output voltage. A voltage-to-output transfer function cannot be compared with a duty-to-output one. The gain from duty to voltage must be inside the model. The live session uses a PLECS switching model in place of the Python reference.

6.2 Results

Normalized RMS error against the switching reference, over 20 ms:

Operating point B′: linearized at actual D B: linearized at D = 0.5 A: passive LC
D = 0.2 2.0 % 103 % 102 %
D = 0.5 2.7 % 2.7 % 34 %
D = 0.8 4.1 % 54 % 54 %

The averaged model is accurate when it is linearized at the right point. The large errors come from the operating point, not from averaging. The passive LC model fails even at D = 0.5, where its gain was matched. Its inductance is not reflected, so its resonance is at 503 Hz, not 252 Hz.

6.3 A larger perturbation

Repeat the D = 0.8 test with larger duty steps. Compare the final value of the linear model with the exact new operating point :

Duty step Linear prediction Exact change Linear error
0.005 12.5 V 12.8 V −2.5 %
0.02 50.0 V 55.6 V −10 %
0.05 125 V 167 V −25 %

This is linearization error. The nonlinear averaged model (3.2) has no such error, because it predicts the exact final value. At D = 0.8 the conversion ratio is steep and curved, so the linear model is local in a strict sense.

6.4 Toward the switching frequency

Ask. What happens when the crossover moves toward the switching frequency?

The averaged model starts to fail, and several effects appear that no model above contains: the modulator delay, the sampling of a digital controller, aliasing and the ripple in the measured signal. A first estimate treats the total effect as a pure delay :

(6.1)
Crossover Delay Extra phase lag
2 kHz 50 µs 36°
2 kHz 75 µs 54°
500 Hz 75 µs 13.5°

At 20 kHz, 75 µs is 1.5 switching periods. This value is common for a digital controller that computes for one period and updates the PWM once per period. It is an estimate, not a rule. Take from the actual sampling and PWM implementation.

An averaged model can describe the low-frequency behaviour well and still miss the effects that limit the achievable bandwidth. When the crossover reaches a significant fraction of , a sampled-data model is the next step. Corradini, Maksimović, Mattavelli and Zane develop it for digital control of converters.

7. Quick check and conclusion

Answer true or false, and give one sentence of reason.

  1. Pole placement requires an LC-only model.
  2. In an ideal CCM buck with constant input voltage, the duty cycle changes the open-loop LC poles.
  3. In an ideal CCM boost, the duty cycle changes the plant dynamics.
  4. A basic averaged model captures PWM delay and sampling effects.
  5. A linearized model can be accurate at one operating point and inaccurate at another.

Now return to the three predictions of §1. Change any answer that this lesson contradicts, and name the section that changed it.

Who was telling the truth? Both engineers can be right. Each must know what the model includes, what it excludes, and over which range it stays valid. Three principles summarize the lesson:

  1. A model is not the system. Its validity follows from the assumptions used to derive it.
  2. The design method does not decide the model's accuracy. Pole placement on a correctly linearized converter model is good power-electronics practice.
  3. Match the model to the question. An LC model is enough for a buck or an inverter with a stiff link. A boost or buck-boost needs the duty-dependent averaged model. A loop near the switching frequency needs a sampled-data model.

A correct controller cannot compensate for a fundamentally wrong model. Robust feedback tolerates model error, but only within its stability and performance margins.

8. What to retain

  1. Pole placement designs controllers. Small-signal modeling builds plants. The disagreement is about the plant, never about the method.
  2. Ask whether d multiplies a state. In the ideal buck it does not, so the LC model is exact. In the boost and buck-boost it does, so the reflected inductance and the RHP zero move with the operating point.
  3. The RHP zero is physical. The output first moves the wrong way. It limits the crossover, and no stable controller can remove it.
  4. Gains designed at one duty cycle are a different controller at another. Check the worst operating point, not only the design point.
  5. Separate the errors. Operating-point error comes from a fixed linearization. Linearization error grows with the perturbation. Averaging error and delay grow as the bandwidth approaches .
  6. Neither basic model sees the switching frequency. Add the delay, then a sampled-data model, before trusting a fast loop.

9. Training: problem-driven exercises

As in Lessons 1 and 2, start each exercise with a prediction. Choose a model, solve, compare the alternatives and defend a decision. For every exercise, state your choice, one benefit and one cost. Name the condition or measurement that would change your choice.

  • T1 is worked here, all seven parts included.
  • E1 and E2 are assigned Exercises. This lesson shows their first four parts. Their Solution is held in the Enrolled companion and released after the deadline.

Every Problem states its own operating point. Never carry a number from one operating point to another.

T1 — Is the bare LC model of the boost good enough?

Problem

A control engineer must design the voltage loop of the §4 boost at D = 0.5: 100 V in, 1 mH, 100 µF, 100 Ω. The engineer models the plant as the bare LC filter with L = 1 mH and matches its DC gain to the boost. The planned crossover is 50 Hz, to be raised later to 1 kHz. Is the bare LC model good enough? If not, what is the smallest change that makes it good enough?

Predict. Will the bare LC model put the resonance too high or too low? By how much?

Why we do it

Most control engineers meet power electronics through the inverter, where the LC model works (§5.1). This exercise finds the exact point at which their habit fails in a DC/DC converter. It also shows that the fix can be small.

What matters

  • Compare the resonance and the phase of the two models. The DC gain is matched by construction.
  • The averaged model has a zero that the LC model cannot have.
  • The planned crossover decides which errors matter. An error far above crossover changes little.

Where it appears in practice

PFC boost stages, battery boost converters and photovoltaic MPPT boosts are often controlled by engineers trained on drives or inverters. The same check applies to every interleaved and multiphase boost.

Possible solutions

(a) Keep the bare LC model. Its poles are at = 503 Hz with Q = 31.6. The averaged model has them at = 252 Hz with Q = 15.8 (§4.4). The resonance is a factor of 2 = 1/D′ too high. In the step test of §6.2 this model is 34 % wrong even at D = 0.5.

(b) Reflect the inductor. Use = 4 mH in the LC model. Then the poles and Q are exact, because the denominator of (4.6) is the LC polynomial with . Only the RHP zero at 3.98 kHz is missing.

(c) Use the full averaged model (4.6). It adds the RHP zero. It is exact at D = 0.5 to the accuracy of §6.2: 2.7 % RMS error.

(d) Use a switching simulation. It needs no derivation, but it gives no transfer function to design with.

Pros and cons

Model Benefit Cost
(a) bare LC Familiar; no operating point needed Resonance wrong by 1/D′; no RHP zero
(b) reflected LC One line of change; exact poles Valid only at one D; still no RHP zero
(c) averaged Exact at its operating point; shows the RHP zero Must be re-linearized when D changes
(d) switching Includes ripple, and delay if modelled No transfer function; slow to iterate

Conclusion

At 50 Hz, (b) is sufficient. The RHP zero at 3.98 kHz is 80 times above crossover, and its phase lag at 50 Hz is = 0.7°. At 1 kHz the same zero costs = 14° of phase. That is too much to ignore, and the crossover is above the one-fifth rule of §4.5, so use (c). If the boost must also run at D = 0.8, the zero falls to 637 Hz, and a 1 kHz crossover is not possible at all. Then the decision is not about the model. The requirement must change, or the control structure must change, for example to an inner current loop. Use (d) to confirm the final design, not to create it.

E1 — One state-feedback controller for the whole duty range?

Problem

The §4 buck-boost (100 V in, 1 mH, 100 µF, 100 Ω, 50 kHz) must regulate its output from 25 V to 400 V, so D runs from 0.2 to 0.8. A designer places the closed-loop poles at 500 Hz, = 0.7, at D = 0.5, using duty-unit state feedback on the averaged model.

  1. Derive the linearized buck-boost model (4.8) and compute the gains and N at D = 0.5.
  2. Keep the gains fixed. Find the closed-loop poles, the step overshoot or undershoot and the DC gain at D = 0.2 and D = 0.8.
  3. Compare two remedies: (a) schedule the gains with D, so the poles are at 500 Hz, = 0.7 at every D; (b) keep fixed gains, but choose a slower target of 150 Hz, = 0.7, at D = 0.5. Test both at D = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.
  4. Locate the RHP zero at each D. Say which remedy it limits and why.

Predict. Which remedy is safer: faster scheduled gains, or slower fixed gains?

Why we do it

§4.6 shows the boost result. This exercise asks for a decision. A slower controller usually feels safer, but this plant can show otherwise. The task is to find out before the hardware does.

What matters

  • Use the linearized model at each D. Do not reuse a matrix from another operating point.
  • Report real closed-loop poles as two frequencies, not as one and .
  • Check stability first. Overshoot and DC gain mean nothing for an unstable loop.
  • Gain scheduling needs a measured or estimated D. Name what you would measure.

Where it appears in practice

Wide-range converters: battery chargers, LED drivers, photovoltaic and fuel-cell converters, and the inverting buck-boost stages of portable equipment. Commercial controllers solve the same problem with current-mode control and input-voltage feedforward.

Solution

Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.

E2 — How stiff must the DC link be?

Problem

The §5 inverter (1 mH, 20 µF, 50 Ω output filter) runs at a DC operating point M = 0.8. Its DC link is fed from 400 V through a source resistance into a link capacitor . Consider = 0.5, 2 and 10 Ω, and = 50 µF and 500 µF.

  1. Write the three-state averaged model with the states , and . Find the operating point.
  2. Linearize and find the filter resonance, its damping and the DC-link pole for each of the six combinations.
  3. Compare each result with the stiff-link LC model (1125 Hz, = 0.071). For a voltage loop that crosses at 300 Hz, decide which combinations allow the stiff-link model.
  4. Explain why a larger brings the filter back to the stiff-link values, and what it costs.

Predict. Which matters more for the filter resonance: or ?

Why we do it

The stiff-link assumption is the reason why the simple inverter model works (§5.1). This exercise turns that assumption into a check with numbers, so you can defend it or reject it.

What matters

  • The link voltage at the operating point falls with . Use it in the linearization.
  • Two different questions: does the filter move, and how slow is the new DC-link pole?
  • A pole far from crossover can still matter for a slow outer loop or for the upstream converter.

Where it appears in practice

Inverters fed from long DC cables, from batteries with high internal resistance, or from an upstream PFC stage with its own voltage loop. The same coupling explains interactions between cascaded converters.

Solution

Released after the deadline in the Enrolled companion.
